title: Min Cost to Connect All Points
description:
You are given an array `points` representing integer coordinates of some points on a 2D-plane, where `points[i] = [xi, yi]`.

The cost of connecting two points `[xi, yi]` and `[xj, yj]` is the Manhattan distance between them: `|xi - xj| + |yi - yj|`, where `|val|` denotes the absolute value of `val`.

Return the minimum cost to make all points connected. All points are connected if there is exactly one simple path between any two points (a spanning tree). If there is only one point, the minimum cost is `0`.
hints: Model the points as vertices of a complete undirected weighted graph where the edge weight between points i and j is their Manhattan distance.
The problem asks for the total weight of a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) on this dense complete graph.
Because the graph is complete with n <= 1000, an array-based Prim's algorithm runs in O(n^2) time and O(n) extra space without materializing all O(n^2) edges.

examples.explanation: We can connect the points with edges (0,0)-(2,2) [cost 4], (2,2)-(5,2) [cost 3], (5,2)-(7,0) [cost 4], and (2,2)-(3,10) [cost 9] for a total minimum cost of 4 + 3 + 4 + 9 = 20.
Connect (3,12) to (-2,5) with cost 12 and (-2,5) to (-4,1) with cost 6 for a total cost of 18.
Connect (0,0) to (1,0) [cost 1], (1,0) to (1,1) [cost 1], and (1,1) to (-1,1) [cost 2] for a total cost of 4.

title: Connecting Cities With Minimum Cost
description:
There are `n` cities labeled from `1` to `n`. You are given the integer `n` and an array `connections` where `connections[i] = [xi, yi, costi]` indicates that the cost of connecting city `xi` and city `yi` (bidirectional connection) is `costi`.

Return the minimum cost to connect all the `n` cities such that there is at least one path between each pair of cities. If it is impossible to connect all the `n` cities, return `-1`.

The cost is the sum of the connections' costs used. Note that multiple connections may exist between the same pair of cities, and `connections` may be empty. If `n == 1`, all cities are already connected with cost `0`.
hints: Think of cities as vertices and connections as undirected weighted edges; you want the weight of a Minimum Spanning Tree.
Sort all connections by cost in ascending order and greedily add an edge whenever it connects two previously disconnected components.
Use a Disjoint Set Union (Union-Find) data structure with path compression and union by rank/size; after processing edges, verify that all n cities form a single connected component.

examples.explanation: Choosing edges [2,3,1] and [1,2,5] connects all 3 cities with minimum total cost 1 + 5 = 6.
Cities {1, 2} and {3, 4} cannot be connected into a single component, so return -1.
Choose edges [1,2,1], [2,3,2], and [3,4,3] (or [1,2,1], [1,3,2], and [3,4,3]) for a total minimum cost of 6.

title: Optimize Water Distribution in a Village
description:
There are `n` houses in a village, numbered from `1` to `n`. We want to supply water for all the houses by building wells and laying pipes.

For each house `i` (`1 <= i <= n`), we can either build a well inside it directly with cost `wells[i - 1]` (0-indexed), or pipe in water from another house that has water. The costs to lay pipes between houses are given by the array `pipes`, where each `pipes[j] = [house1j, house2j, costj]` represents the cost to connect `house1j` and `house2j` together using a bidirectional pipe.

Note that there may be multiple valid connections between the same two houses with different costs.

Return the minimum total cost to supply water to all houses.
hints: Every connected component of piped houses must contain at least one well.
Introduce a virtual water-source node 0 and add an edge of weight wells[i - 1] between node 0 and each house i.
Now supplying water to every house is equivalent to finding a Minimum Spanning Tree on the (n + 1)-node graph using Kruskal's or Prim's algorithm.

examples.explanation: Build a well in house 1 (cost 1) and connect houses 1-2 (cost 1) and 2-3 (cost 1) via pipes for a total cost of 3.
We can either build a well in each house (1 + 1 = 2) or build one well and connect them with the pipe of cost 1 (1 + 1 = 2).
Pipes are more expensive than building wells directly, so build a well in every house for a total cost of 5 + 5 + 5 = 15.

title: Find Critical and Pseudo-Critical Edges in Minimum Spanning Tree
description:
Given a weighted undirected connected graph with `n` vertices numbered from `0` to `n - 1`, and an array `edges` where `edges[i] = [ai, bi, weighti]` represents a bidirectional and weighted edge between nodes `ai` and `bi`. A minimum spanning tree (MST) is a subset of the graph's edges that connects all vertices without cycles and with the minimum possible total edge weight.

Find all the critical and pseudo-critical edges in the given graph's minimum spanning tree (MST):
- A **critical edge** is an MST edge whose deletion from the graph would cause the MST weight to increase (or disconnect the graph so no spanning tree exists).
- A **pseudo-critical edge** is an edge that can appear in some MSTs, but not all (it is not critical, yet there exists at least one MST containing it).

Return a list `[critical, pseudoCritical]` containing the 0-based indices of all critical edges and all pseudo-critical edges respectively. **Sort each of the two lists in ascending order of edge index.**
hints: First sort the edges by weight (preserving their original indices) and run Kruskal's algorithm to compute the baseline MST weight.
An edge i is critical if running Kruskal's algorithm while skipping edge i fails to connect all n vertices or yields a strictly larger spanning tree weight.
If edge i is not critical, force-include it first in DSU and run Kruskal's on the remaining edges; if the resulting spanning tree has the exact baseline MST weight, then edge i is pseudo-critical.

examples.explanation: The MST weight is 7. Removing edge 0 or edge 1 increases the MST weight, so [0, 1] are critical. Edges 2, 3, 4, and 5 each appear in some MSTs of weight 7 but not all, while edge 6 (weight 6) never appears in any MST.
All four edges have weight 1 forming a 4-cycle; any 3 edges form an MST of weight 3, so no edge is critical and all four edges [0, 1, 2, 3] are pseudo-critical.
The unique MST uses edges 0 and 1 (total weight 3). Both are critical, and edge 2 (weight 5) is never part of any MST.

title: Minimum Spanning Tree Total Weight
description:
Given an undirected weighted graph with `n` vertices labeled from `0` to `n - 1` and an array `edges` where `edges[i] = [u, v, w]` represents an undirected edge between vertices `u` and `v` with non-negative weight `w`.

The graph may contain **self-loops** (`u == v`) and **parallel edges** (multiple edges between the same pair of vertices with possibly different weights), and it may be disconnected.

Find and return the total weight of a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) connecting all `n` vertices. If the graph is disconnected and no spanning tree exists, return `-1`. For `n == 1`, a single vertex is already a valid spanning tree of total weight `0` (self-loops are never included in a spanning tree). Note that the total weight may exceed the 32-bit signed integer range, so return a 64-bit integer (`long`).
hints: Build an adjacency list for all edges (ignoring self-loops where u == v) and grow the MST from vertex 0 using Prim's algorithm with a min-heap.
At each step, pop the minimum-weight edge leading to an unvisited vertex, mark that vertex visited, add the weight to a 64-bit accumulator, and push all outgoing edges to unvisited neighbors.
If fewer than n vertices are visited when the heap becomes empty, the graph is disconnected so return -1.

examples.explanation: Pick edges (1,2,1), (1,3,2), and (0,2,3) to connect all 4 vertices with minimum total weight 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.
Vertices {0, 1} and {2, 3} are in separate connected components, so no spanning tree exists and we return -1.
Ignore the self-loop (0,0,1) and the heavier parallel edge (0,1,10). Choosing (0,1,3) and (1,2,4) gives total weight 7.

title: Remove Max Number of Edges to Keep Graph Fully Traversable
description:
Alice and Bob have an undirected graph of `n` nodes labeled from `1` to `n` and three types of edges:
- Type `1`: Can be traversed by Alice only.
- Type `2`: Can be traversed by Bob only.
- Type `3`: Can be traversed by both Alice and Bob.

Given an array `edges` where `edges[i] = [typei, ui, vi]` represents a bidirectional edge of type `typei` between nodes `ui` and `vi`, find the maximum number of edges you can remove so that after removing the edges, the graph can still be fully traversed by both Alice and Bob. The graph is fully traversable by Alice and Bob if starting from any node, they can reach all other nodes.

Return the maximum number of edges you can remove, or return `-1` if Alice and Bob cannot fully traverse the graph.
constraints: All tuples (typei, ui, vi) are distinct.
hints: Maximizing the number of removed edges is equivalent to minimizing the number of edges kept so that both Alice and Bob have a spanning tree.
Always prioritize Type 3 edges first, because a single Type 3 edge that merges two components helps both Alice and Bob simultaneously instead of needing one Type 1 edge and one Type 2 edge.
Maintain two Disjoint Set Union structures (one for Alice, one for Bob): first process all Type 3 edges, then process Type 1 edges on Alice's DSU and Type 2 edges on Bob's DSU.

examples.explanation: If we remove the 2 edges [1,1,2] and [1,1,3], the remaining 4 edges still allow both Alice and Bob to traverse all 4 nodes. Removing any more makes the graph untraversable.
All 4 edges are required: the two Type 3 edges connect {1,2,3}, while node 4 needs both the Type 1 edge for Alice and the Type 2 edge for Bob. So 0 edges can be removed.
Alice cannot reach node 4 and Bob cannot reach node 1, so the graph cannot be fully traversed by both; return -1.

title: Minimum Bottleneck Spanning Tree
description: Given a connected undirected weighted graph, choose a spanning tree that minimizes its largest edge weight. Return the minimum possible largest edge weight.
hints: Sort candidate edges by weight and use a disjoint-set structure to track connected components.
Respect the stated tie-breaking rule and handle disconnected graphs if allowed.

solutionCode.java: class Solution { int f(int[]p,int x){while(p[x]!=x){p[x]=p[p[x]];x=p[x];}return x;} public int minimumBottleneck(int n,int[][]e){if(n==1)return 0;Arrays.sort(e,(a,b)->Integer.compare(a[2],b[2]));int[]p=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++)p[i]=i;for(int[]x:e){int a=f(p,x[0]),b=f(p,x[1]);if(a!=b){p[a]=b;if(--n==1)return x[2];}}return -1;} }

title: Maximum Spacing for K Clusters
description: Partition the vertices of a connected undirected weighted graph into exactly `k` non-empty clusters. The spacing is the minimum edge weight joining two different clusters. Return the maximum spacing achievable. Return -1 when `k` is 1 or `n` is 1 because the spacing is undefined.
hints: Sort candidate edges by weight and use a disjoint-set structure to track connected components.
Respect the stated tie-breaking rule and handle disconnected graphs if allowed.

solutionCode.java: class Solution { int f(int[]p,int x){while(p[x]!=x){p[x]=p[p[x]];x=p[x];}return x;}public int maximumSpacing(int n,int k,int[][]e){if(k<=1||n<=1)return -1;Arrays.sort(e,(a,b)->Integer.compare(a[2],b[2]));int[]p=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++)p[i]=i;int c=n;for(int[]x:e){int a=f(p,x[0]),b=f(p,x[1]);if(a!=b){if(c==k)return x[2];p[a]=b;c--;}}return -1;} }

title: Minimum Bottleneck Path Queries
description: For every query `[u,v]`, find a path from `u` to `v` that minimizes the largest edge weight on the path. Return that minimum largest-edge weight, or -1 if no path exists. The answer for `u == v` is 0.
hints: Sort candidate edges by weight and use a disjoint-set structure to track connected components.
Respect the stated tie-breaking rule and handle disconnected graphs if allowed.

solutionCode.java: class Solution { public int[] minimaxPathQueries(int n,int[][]e,int[][]q){int inf=1000000000;int[][]d=new int[n][n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++){Arrays.fill(d[i],inf);d[i][i]=0;}for(int[]x:e){d[x[0]][x[1]]=Math.min(d[x[0]][x[1]],x[2]);d[x[1]][x[0]]=Math.min(d[x[1]][x[0]],x[2]);}for(int k=0;k<n;k++)for(int i=0;i<n;i++)for(int j=0;j<n;j++)d[i][j]=Math.min(d[i][j],Math.max(d[i][k],d[k][j]));int[]a=new int[q.length];for(int i=0;i<q.length;i++)a[i]=d[q[i][0]][q[i][1]]==inf?-1:d[q[i][0]][q[i][1]];return a;} }

title: Minimum Spanning Forest Weight
description: Given an undirected weighted graph that may be disconnected, return the minimum total weight of a spanning forest: a minimum spanning tree for each connected component. Ignore self-loops and redundant edges.
hints: Sort candidate edges by weight and use a disjoint-set structure to track connected components.
Respect the stated tie-breaking rule and handle disconnected graphs if allowed.

solutionCode.java: class Solution { int f(int[]p,int x){while(p[x]!=x){p[x]=p[p[x]];x=p[x];}return x;}public int minimumForestWeight(int n,int[][]e){Arrays.sort(e,(a,b)->Integer.compare(a[2],b[2]));int[]p=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++)p[i]=i;int s=0;for(int[]x:e){int a=f(p,x[0]),b=f(p,x[1]);if(a!=b){p[a]=b;s+=x[2];}}return s;} }

title: Minimum Spanning Tree Edge Indices
description: Given a connected undirected weighted graph, return the input indices of the edges in a minimum spanning tree. Kruskal’s algorithm must break equal-weight ties by smaller input index. Return selected indices in increasing input order.
hints: Sort candidate edges by weight and use a disjoint-set structure to track connected components.
Respect the stated tie-breaking rule and handle disconnected graphs if allowed.

solutionCode.java: class Solution { int f(int[]p,int x){while(p[x]!=x){p[x]=p[p[x]];x=p[x];}return x;}public List<Integer> minimumSpanningTreeEdges(int n,int[][]e){Integer[]idx=new Integer[e.length];for(int i=0;i<e.length;i++)idx[i]=i;Arrays.sort(idx,(i,j)->{int c=Integer.compare(e[i][2],e[j][2]);return c!=0?c:Integer.compare(i,j);});int[]p=new int[n];for(int i=0;i<n;i++)p[i]=i;List<Integer>out=new ArrayList<>();for(int i:idx){int a=f(p,e[i][0]),b=f(p,e[i][1]);if(a!=b){p[a]=b;out.add(i);}}if(out.size()!=n-1)return new ArrayList<>();Collections.sort(out);return out;} }
